text: You're in the supermarket, pushing your cart. Aisles feel so wide. You just want essentials quickly, but there's so much empty room. It seems inefficient, right?
You navigate around other shoppers. This extra width means longer walks, making your quick trip feel slower. What's the real purpose of all this space?
You might guess it's for accessibility or to avoid congestion. Perhaps bad design. Your mind searches for a simple reason, but it just doesn't quite fit.
Wide aisles aren't for *your* speed. They optimize customer flow and *dwell time*. This space encourages you to slow down, browse, and notice more products.
The cost? More browsing means more temptation. You pick up unplanned items, adding them to your cart. Wide aisles quietly encourage impulse purchases.
Next time, that spacious feeling isn't accidental. It's a designed system, subtly influencing your shopping. You now understand *why* they're built that way.
